analysis.one_liner: Limits Espionage Act prosecutions to cleared insiders and protects journalists and whistleblowers who expose government wrongdoing.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the House in March 2026 with eight Democratic backers, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote while Congress remains in session.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill narrows the Espionage Act, the World War I-era law the government has used to prosecute people who handle leaked defense information. It would make it much harder to charge a whistleblower or a journalist: only people who held authorized access to classified information and signed a nondisclosure agreement, or true foreign agents, could be prosecuted, and prosecutors would have to prove the defendant specifically meant to injure the United States or help a foreign nation. It also gives defendants the right to tell a jury why they acted and a defense when their disclosure revealed illegal conduct, gross waste, abuse of authority, or a danger to public health and safety.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal employees and contractors with security clearances who report official wrongdoing, journalists and newsrooms that publish leaked national-security information, and members of the public who learn about government misconduct they would otherwise never see.

how_it_helps.text: Prosecution under the Espionage Act's main sections (18 U.S.C. 793 and 798) would be limited to 'covered persons' — people who were granted official access to classified information and signed a nondisclosure agreement — plus, in one provision, foreign agents, so journalists and ordinary recipients of leaked information could no longer be charged.

The government would have to prove a defendant acted 'with specific intent to injure the United States or advantage any foreign nation,' replacing the much looser standard that someone acted with 'intent or reason to believe' the information could be used to the country's detriment.

Defendants would gain the right to testify to a jury about their purpose, and a new affirmative defense would protect anyone whose disclosure revealed a violation of law, gross mismanagement, gross waste of funds, abuse of authority, or a substantial and specific danger to public health or safety.
The government would also have to show the information in question was 'properly classified,' so an agency could not prosecute over information that was wrongly stamped secret.

analysis.who_pays: The executive branch — especially intelligence and defense agencies — would lose its broadest criminal tool for punishing and deterring unauthorized disclosures, including cases where leaked information caused no real harm, and would face litigation over whether documents were properly classified.

drawbacks.text: The bill reaches only 'covered persons' and foreign agents, so a person who obtained defense information without official authorization — and who does not qualify as an agent of a foreign power — could no longer be prosecuted under section 793 for possessing or spreading it.

The affirmative defense is broad: it covers disclosure of a violation of 'any law, rule, or regulation,' so a defendant could invoke it based on a technical rule breach rather than a serious abuse, and juries would have to weigh the whistleblower's purpose against any damage the disclosure caused.

Requiring proof that information was 'properly classified' would push espionage prosecutions into fights over classification decisions, which could complicate cases involving genuinely damaging leaks; genuine foreign agents would still be prosecutable, but the bill shrinks the deterrence the current law provides against leaks by people outside the cleared system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real gap: under current law a journalist or blogger who merely receives leaked defense information can face the same felony charges as a spy, and a whistleblower who exposes illegal conduct has no defense no matter how serious the abuse. The trade-off is real too — the bill makes it harder to prosecute leaks by people outside the cleared system and forces every case into litigation over intent and classification validity. On balance, the protections it gives whistleblowers and the press outweigh the narrowed deterrence, especially since foreign agents remain fully prosecutable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it has received no hearing, markup, or vote while Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the bill on March 12, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
Seven Democratic representatives signed on as cosponsors — Reps. Garcia of Illinois, Lee of Pennsylvania, Norton, Omar, Ramirez, and Thanedar — and no Republican has joined.

The bill rewrites the two core Espionage Act statutes (18 U.S.C. 793 and 798) to raise the intent requirement, limit who can be prosecuted, require proof of proper classification, and add a purpose-testimony right and a public-interest affirmative defense.
No further action has been recorded since the referral to Judiciary, and the Congress does not end until January 2027, so the bill is still technically alive but has no scheduled path to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nobody has moved it at all, which leaves in place the existing Espionage Act as written — the version that lets the executive branch charge journalists and recipients of leaks on a low intent standard and gives whistleblowers no defense for exposing misconduct. The intelligence and defense establishment is better off with the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The executive branch's current leak-prosecution power

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 12, 2026, naming it after whistleblower Daniel Ellsberg and drafting it to narrow the Espionage Act and add a public-interest defense.

for.name: Six Democratic House cosponsors
for.role: Reps. Garcia (IL), Lee (PA), Norton (DC), Omar (MN), Ramirez (IL), and Thanedar (MI)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill at introduction; no other members have joined since.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Rep. Jim Jordan, chair)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 12, 2026 and has taken no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor — the bill's author plus seven original cosponsors — is a Democrat, and no Republican has signed on, so its support so far is entirely one-sided.

industries.industry: Intelligence and defense agencies (the classified-information establishment)
industries.note: The bill shrinks the statutes these agencies rely on to prosecute leaks: only cleared insiders and foreign agents could be charged, prosecutors would need specific intent to injure the United States, and a public-interest disclosure would be an affirmative defense. Their interest in keeping prosecutions broad runs against the public's interest in learning about official misconduct.

Because prosecution would be limited to people who held authorized access and signed a nondisclosure agreement, reporters and newsrooms could no longer be charged under the Espionage Act for obtaining or publishing leaked defense information — a legal threat that currently hangs over national-security reporting.

Insiders who disclose classified information would still be prosecutable, but only with proof of specific intent to harm the United States, and they would gain an affirmative defense when the disclosure revealed legal violations, gross waste, abuse of authority, or a danger to public health or safety. Malicious leakers lose nothing they should keep; whistleblowers gain the protection they currently lack.

analysis.trajectory: With entirely Democratic sponsorship, no Republican cosponsors, and a Republican-led Judiciary Committee that has taken no action since the referral, the bill is likely to sit without a hearing or vote for the rest of this Congress, as most referred House bills do. Its best realistic paths are a hearing on Espionage Act reform or having provisions folded into a larger bill, neither of which is currently scheduled.
